summary:
SparkShield is a web app that helps spacecraft stowage engineers and mission controllers see the fire risk of every stowed item and fix it before it becomes a problem.

Engineers lay out a ship module by module and stow items in each. SparkShield scores every module for both mission phases, in-space cruise and a Moon or Mars surface stay. The scores come from 339 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics microgravity combustion tests, compared against each phase’s cabin oxygen level. It explains why a space is risky, then suggests fixes and item moves, each re-scored to show how much risk it removes. Code computes every score; AI only writes plain-language explanations, which are checked against the data.

During a mission, an officer can send a fix to an astronaut as a clear stowage instruction. The astronaut marks it done, and the officer sees the confirmation. Engineers can also export a printable handoff report.

This matters because fire in a sealed spacecraft is among the most dangerous emergencies, with nowhere to go. SparkShield turns scattered NASA data into fast, traceable decisions, from planning to the lunar surface.
details:
SparkShield is a fire-risk planner for spacecraft stowage. An engineer chooses a ship (ISS-style station, transit spacecraft or a custom hull) and stows items in each module: materials like clothing, foam and acrylic, machinery like laptops and battery packs, and safety gear. They set the mission conditions for two phases: in-space cruise at 0 g and 21% oxygen, and a Moon or Mars surface stay with a higher-oxygen cabin.

SparkShield then scores every module and the whole ship from 0 to 100 for both phases, on a five-level scale from Low to Severe. For each module it shows what drives the risk and what fixes it: swap a material, add a detector or extinguisher, or move an item somewhere safer. Every suggestion is re-scored before it’s shown, so the engineer sees the real point drop. A built-in assistant answers questions about the result and cites the specific NASA experiments behind its answers.

How it works

  • Scoring data: we cleaned 339 burn/no-burn results from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion experiments: FLEX, BASS-II, ACME and Saffire I–III.
  • Material hazard: for each material, the tests show the oxygen level where it starts to burn. The hazard rises the further the cabin’s oxygen is above that threshold.
  • Module score: combines material hazard, fuel load, ignition and oxygen sources nearby, airflow and material thickness, with credit for detectors and extinguishers.
  • Ship score: combines the riskiest module and the average, then both mission phases.
  • Untested items: get an estimate from their flammability level and are labelled “no NASA test data”.
  • AI: Google Gemini writes the explanations only. Its text is checked automatically: every number, experiment ID and link must exist in the data, and it may not blame factors the score doesn’t include. If a check fails, the app uses template text.

Mission workflow

  • Engineer mode: edit the layout. Modules can be added, moved and deleted within a fixed hull.
  • Plan sign-off: recorded for materials (M&P) and safety (S&MA) review. In the demo it’s a button, not a real reviewer approval.
  • Crew instructions: a mission controller sends an applied fix to an astronaut as a stowage instruction. The astronaut sees an instruction card with the “take out” and “stow here” modules highlighted, marks it stowed, and the controller sees the confirmation.
  • Crew handoff mode: locks the layout so the crew can only change items.
  • Handoff report: a printable PDF with the mission conditions, scores, full stowage manifest, open actions, data gaps and sources, plus a downloadable spreadsheet of the manifest.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Fire risks are caught while planning instead of weeks later in safety review.
  • Every score can be traced to NASA test data, and every fix comes with a reason and its measured effect.
  • During a mission, changes go from mission control to the crew and back as one confirmed loop instead of emails and calls.

The goal is safer stowage decisions, made faster, from launch planning to the lunar surface.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, pytest (52 automated tests).
  • Frontend: React, Vite, JavaScript, CSS.
  • AI: Google Gemini API, with the key in Google Secret Manager.
  • Hosting: Google Cloud Run, live at https://flame-api-32147745125.us-west1.run.app
  • Data: NASA PSI combustion experiments, NASA technical reports and NASA fact sheets.
  • Development: GitHub. We used Anthropic’s Claude as a coding assistant, and our team made the design and technical decisions.

What’s creative about it

  • Focused on one user and one step. Instead of a general fire-safety tool, we built for one person, the stowage engineer, at one step of mission prep: drafting where every item goes. That focus let us build a drafting tool that fits how stowage planning actually works, with a fixed hull, a module-by-module layout and fixes that can be applied in one click.
  • Built for cross-team communication. Stowage plans pass between engineers, materials (M&P) and safety (S&MA) reviewers, mission control and the crew. SparkShield gives them one shared plan: a traceable handoff report for reviewers, a recorded sign-off, and stowage instructions that go from mission control to the astronaut and come back confirmed. These steps usually happen through emails and calls.
  • Code scores, AI explains. The AI never decides a safety number, and its explanations are checked against the NASA data before anyone sees them.
  • Two phases. A placement only counts as safe if it passes both cruise and the higher-oxygen surface stay.
  • Moves avoid risky rooms. Suggested moves never put fuel next to a heater or oxygen outlet, and never make the destination High.

What our team considered

  • Who the user is. We designed for the stowage engineer drafting the plan before launch, then extended it to the people the plan reaches: the inventory and stowage officer in mission control and the astronaut on the surface. Each role sees what it needs; for example, the crew view locks the layout so only items can change.
  • Whether we had enough data to act on. We only score what NASA data supports. The 339 PSI tests cover a limited set of materials, so untested items such as clothing and foam get an estimate and are labelled “no NASA test data”. NASA has no partial-gravity combustion tests yet, so surface scores use microgravity and oxygen-level data, and the app lists this as a data gap. Factors we couldn’t back with data (cabin pressure, EVA-prep periods) are shown but not scored.
  • Which mission phases to cover. We left out launch and focused on the two phases where stowed items sit for weeks or months: in-space cruise (0 g, 21% oxygen) and the Moon or Mars surface stay, where habitats may run higher oxygen. A placement only counts as safe if it passes both, since an item stowed for cruise is still there on the surface.
  • Traceability: each assessment has an ID, and the handoff report lists its sources, so safety reviewers can check every rating.
  • Usability: a fixed hull matches real spacecraft, the crew view is locked so the layout can’t change, and the site works on mobile.
  • Privacy and safety: no personal data, API keys kept in Secret Manager, and a clear note that SparkShield is a research aid, not a safety certification.
